newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Foreign units to bolster Barlow H1.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Foreign units to bolster Barlow H1.

text.p: South African industrial holdings firm Barlow Ltd is set to post modest half-year growth next week as its local operations are hampered by a slowdown in the economy, analysts said on Friday.
However, strong growth from the group's overseas operations, which in 1996 accounted for 25 percent of Barlow's attributable profit, will bolster the figures.
"The growth is mainly from the international side. Within South Africa everything is pretty flat," said one analyst who declined to be identified.
Analysts expected pre-exceptional earnings per share to rise to a range of 150 to 165 cents from 142.5 last time. The consensus figure came in at 160.7 cents, an improvement of less than 13 percent.
The dividend was seen rising to a range of 36.0 to 38.0 from 33.0 cents last time. The consensus figure was 37.1 cents.
The results are due to be announced on Monday.

Analysts said the international operations, such as materials handling and capital equipment, would perform strongly on good demand. Leading the way is a robust performance from British industrials and trading unit J. Bibby and Sons Plc .
But the slowing local economy will hit the firm's wide spread of industrial operations, ranging from steel tubing to lime and cement.
At its year results last November Barlow said that a slowdown in fixed investment spending in South Africa would point to difficult local trading conditions for much of the current financial year.
"One must still be cautious on the local side. It is not looking as rosy as one might like," said Mark Ingham, analyst at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
Some analysts said the steel operation could come in with quite a steep drop in profits as it gets hit by a tough global market and low international prices.
The motor vehicle business is also being squeezed by tight market conditions, as are the paint, construction and cement businesses.

Barlows has exposure to the cement industry through a stake in Pretoria Portland Cement Ltd which recently announced an 11 percent fall in first half earnings per share to 201.9 cents, confounding analysts who had expected a modest increase.
"The market has not taken into account the extent of the economic slowdown," said one analyst whose forecasts were at the bearish end of the expected range for Barlow.
The analyst also said that, while the overseas operations would still grow, they would not benefit as much from the weakness of the rand as they did last year.
